metaData.originalTitle: C++之父开撕 AI Coding：资深开发者宁愿退休也不愿伺候 AI 生成的代码
metaData.title: C++ Creator Takes Aim at AI Coding: Senior Developers Would Rather Retire Than Tending AI-Generated Code
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: In a podcast, C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup sharply criticizes the quality and verification challenges of AI-generated code, while systematically reviewing the design philosophy, standardization history, and engineering practices of the C++ language.
metaData.summary: This article is compiled from an in-depth podcast interview with Bjarne Stroustrup. The core discussion revolves around the limitations of AI programming: Stroustrup points out that code generated by LLMs is bloated, filled with old bugs and security vulnerabilities, and difficult to verify, leading senior developers to choose retirement rather than dealing with the verification work. He also systematically reviews the evolution of C++ over more than four decades, covering language design philosophy (emphasizing type-oriented programming and zero-overhead abstraction), the standardization process (committee consensus mechanism, shuttle diplomacy with IBM/Intel), the memory safety debate (over 90% of vulnerabilities originate from C-style code rather than C++ itself), and advice for beginners. The article also includes vivid narratives about the legendary culture of Bell Labs, interactions with Dennis Ritchie, and the cautionary tale of the Vasa warship.

mainPoints.point: AI-generated code suffers from serious quality and verification issues.
mainPoints.explanation: Stroustrup believes that LLMs are trained on old code, generating bloated code that contains old bugs and security vulnerabilities. Moreover, each modification to the prompt yields different results, making verification extremely costly and causing senior developers to be unwilling to take on the task.

mainPoints.point: C++'s design philosophy is type-oriented and zero-overhead abstraction.
mainPoints.explanation: C++ is not a purely object-oriented language; it emphasizes reducing runtime errors through a strong type system and compile-time resolution, while offering performance comparable to C, and even achieving 'negative overhead' optimization through superior abstractions.

mainPoints.point: Memory safety issues primarily stem from C-style coding, not C++ itself.
mainPoints.explanation: Over 90% of memory safety vulnerabilities come from using raw pointers and C-style code. Modern C++ can avoid these issues through tools like span and vector, and Stroustrup is promoting the Profiles mechanism to enforce safe coding practices.

mainPoints.point: C++ standardization is a consensus-driven democratic process.
mainPoints.explanation: The standards committee requires a supermajority (ideally 90%) to pass features, ensuring language stability and compatibility but also leading to slow evolution. Stroustrup reflects on the need to establish more efficient steering groups.

mainPoints.point: Learning a programming language should be about acquiring the ideas it embodies, not just its syntax.
mainPoints.explanation: Stroustrup advises developers to learn languages that are significantly different from their current ones (such as functional languages) to broaden their horizons, and emphasizes that 'serious programmers' should understand the precision of engineering and mathematics.

keyQuotes: I have already seen some senior developers starting to retire—because they don't want to deal with this kind of verification work anymore: every time you change the code or change the prompt, the generated output changes.
LLMs are trained on old code, so the code they generate imitates old code, resulting in old performance and old bugs.
Thinking that the next version will solve the problem is always a dangerous assumption.
You must first strengthen the foundation, ensuring it is not just a pile of random features, because that is complexity.
What matters is not which languages you learn, but the ideas embedded in those languages; you should learn languages that are different from your current one.
